opencomputers/backups:
A backup configuration names one directory on one host, a schedule, and a retention policy.
Each run produces a snapshot, and a snapshot can be restored onto any host in your organization.

This is the backup path for machines you own. Managed sandboxes and computers use their own [snapshots](/docs/api-reference/snapshots).

## Create a backup configuration

**miosa CLI**

```bash
miosa host backup list <host>
miosa host backup new <host> --name nightly --path /data --schedule "0 3 * * *" --keep 7
miosa host backup new <host> --name logs --path /var/log --schedule "0 * * * *" --compression 6 --exclude "*.tmp"
```

Aliases: `miosa host backups`, and `create` for `new`.

**REST API**

```bash
curl --fail-with-body -sS \
  -X POST "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/opencomputers/hosts/$HOST_ID/backup-configs" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"nightly","path":"/data","schedule_cron":"0 3 * * *","timezone":"UTC","retention_count":7}'
```

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | Yes | 1 to 100 characters; unique per host |
| `path` | string | Yes | Directory on the host to back up, up to 1024 characters |
| `schedule_cron` | string | No | Cron expression, parsed and validated when the configuration is saved |
| `timezone` | string | No | Timezone the schedule is read in; default `UTC` |
| `retention_count` | integer | No | How many snapshots to keep, 1 to 365 |
| `retention_days` | integer | No | How many days to keep snapshots, 1 to 3650 |
| `exclude_patterns` | string[] | No | Globs to exclude |
| `compression_level` | integer | No | 1 to 22; default 19 |

A configuration is `active` or `paused`.
`last_snapshot_at` and `last_snapshot_size_bytes` record the most recent run.

## Run and manage schedules

```bash
miosa host backup trigger <host> nightly
miosa host backup pause <host> nightly
miosa host backup resume <host> nightly
miosa host backup update <host> nightly --schedule "0 4 * * *"
miosa host backup rm <host> nightly --yes
```

| Action | REST |
|---|---|
| Trigger now | `POST .../backup-configs/{config_id}/trigger` |
| Pause | `POST .../backup-configs/{config_id}/pause` |
| Resume | `POST .../backup-configs/{config_id}/resume` |
| Update | `PATCH .../backup-configs/{config_id}` |
| Delete | `DELETE .../backup-configs/{config_id}` |

A trigger returns `202` with the new snapshot while the upload is still running.
Triggering a backup on a host that is not connected returns `503`.

## Snapshots

**miosa CLI**

```bash
miosa host backup snapshot list <host> nightly --limit 10
miosa host backup snapshot list <host> nightly --before 2026-09-01T00:00:00Z
miosa host backup snapshot get <snapshot>
miosa host backup snapshot rm <snapshot> --yes
```

Aliases: `miosa host backup snapshots`.

**REST API**

```bash
curl --fail-with-body -sS \
  "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/opencomputers/hosts/$HOST_ID/backup-configs/$CONFIG_ID/snapshots?limit=10" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"
```

| Snapshot field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `id` | Snapshot ID, used by every snapshot route |
| `config_id` | The configuration that produced it |
| `host_id` | The host it was taken from |
| `state` | `uploading`, `complete`, `failed`, or `expired` |
| `total_bytes` | Uncompressed size |
| `compressed_bytes` | Stored size |
| `chunk_count` | Number of stored chunks |
| `started_at`, `completed_at` | Timing |
| `error` | Failure reason, when `state` is `failed` |

Only a snapshot in state `complete` can be restored.
Snapshot routes are tenant-scoped, so `GET /api/v1/opencomputers/snapshots/{id}` and `DELETE /api/v1/opencomputers/snapshots/{id}` take the snapshot ID alone, without a host.

## Restore a snapshot

**miosa CLI**

```bash
miosa host backup snapshot fork <snapshot> --to-host <host> --to-path /restore
miosa host backup snapshot fork <snapshot> --overwrite
```

`--to-host` defaults to the host the snapshot came from, and `--overwrite` replaces files that already exist.

**REST API**

```bash
curl --fail-with-body -sS \
  -X POST "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/opencomputers/snapshots/$SNAPSHOT_ID/restore" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"target_host_id":"<host-id>","target_path":"/restore","overwrite":false}'
```

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `target_host_id` | string | Yes | Host to write onto |
| `target_path` | string | No | Directory to write into |
| `overwrite` | boolean | No | Replace existing files; default `false` |

A restore returns `202` with a `restore_id`.
It is asynchronous: watch the target host's filesystem or the [audit log](/docs/opencomputers/security#audit-log) to confirm the files landed.

> **Caution: Restoring is a write to a live machine**
>
> A restore writes real files onto a real host. Without `overwrite`, existing files are left alone, and the restore can still leave a partially restored directory if it fails midway.
> Restore into a new path first, compare, and only then replace the live directory.

## What a backup does and does not cover

- It covers the files under one directory tree on one host. It does not image the operating system, and it does not capture running process state.
- It does not back up a database consistently on its own. Quiesce or dump the database into the backed-up directory before the schedule runs, or use the database's own backup tooling.
- It is not a substitute for a plan that covers losing the machine itself. Keep the credentials and configuration needed to rebuild the host somewhere other than the host.
opencomputers/billing:
Your machine is your own bill. You pay for the hardware, the power, the network, and the hosting, and MIOSA does not charge you for the machine.
MIOSA charges for platform usage at the rates on the [pricing page](https://miosa.ai/pricing); your plan sets limits, never the price.

This page covers the limits that a plan puts on OpenComputers, and the operational caps that apply to everyone.

## Plan limits

Plan limits are per organization.

| Plan | Hosts | Container and compose service slots | Tunnels per host |
|---|---|---|---|
| Developer | 3 | 2 | 0 |
| Business | 50 | 250 | 50 |
| Enterprise | 500 | 1000 | 500 |

Registering past a limit returns `402` with `error: "plan_limit_reached"`, plus the `limit` and `current` values.

A compose project counts its services against the same container budget, so a project with three services uses three slots.

> **Note: Read the limit from the error, not from this table**
>
> Plan limits are enforced by the platform and can change between releases.
> The authoritative value is the one in the `402` response, and the one the UI shows for your organization.

To raise a limit, contact support with your expected scale. See [Support](/docs/support).

## Operational limits

These apply regardless of plan.

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Command length in a job | 1 to 8192 characters |
| Arguments per job | 256 |
| Working directory length | 4096 characters |
| Job timeout | 1 to 3600 seconds; default 30 |
| Exec stream timeout | 30000 ms |
| File transfer chunk | 4 MiB per read or write |
| Backup chunk | 8 MiB compressed |
| Backup compression level | 1 to 22; default 19 |
| Backup retention | 1 to 365 snapshots, or 1 to 3650 days |
| Tunnel frame | 4 MiB |
| Tunnel connect timeout | 10 s |
| Tunnel response timeout | 30 s |
| Forwarded request headers per tunnel request | 64 |
| Container stats tick | 10 s |
| Mesh size | 253 hosts |
| Tags per host | 20 |
| Device browser token TTL | 3600 s |

Job commands are also recorded in audit truncated to 512 characters, and environment variable names are recorded without their values.

## Counters you can read

The platform meters usage per resource, and the counters are on the records you already fetch.

| Counter | Where |
|---|---|
| Host egress and ingress bytes | `usage.lifetime_bytes_egress` and `usage.lifetime_bytes_ingress` on the host record |
| Tunnel requests and bytes | `request_count`, `lifetime_bytes_ingress`, and `lifetime_bytes_egress` on the tunnel |
| Snapshot size | `total_bytes` and `compressed_bytes` on the snapshot |
| Container resource use | `last_cpu_percent`, `last_mem_mb`, and `last_stats_at` on the container |

For the platform-wide picture, use the [Pricing and limits](/docs/pricing) page and the [Usage Rollup API](/docs/api-reference/usage-rollup).

- [Pricing and limits](/docs/pricing): Billable states, machine sizes, and the platform-wide caps.
- [Containers](/docs/opencomputers/containers): Run and watch containers against the container slot budget.
- [Backups and snapshots](/docs/opencomputers/backups): Retention, compression, and restore.
- [Support](/docs/support): Ask for a higher limit with your expected scale.
opencomputers/connect:
Enroll a machine you operate as an OpenComputer.
Your first success is a completed `hostname` command on that exact machine, followed by a verified service restart.
A saved key or an online badge alone is not the finish line.

## Before you start

- Outbound HTTPS and WebSocket access on port 443, including access to GitHub release downloads and `api.miosa.ai`.
- Shell access as the user that should run the agent, plus `curl` and a POSIX shell on Linux or macOS.
- A MIOSA account with access to OpenComputers, and either the `miosa` CLI or a platform API key authorized for the intended organization.
- `sudo` access and systemd if you follow the Linux background-service section.

Choose the agent's OS user deliberately: its permissions determine which local files and services the host can reach.
See the [security model](/docs/opencomputers/security) before connecting sensitive workloads.

> **Note: Prebuilt targets are not universal**
>
> The prebuilt Linux agent target is x86-64.
> On Linux ARM64, or on a platform with no prebuilt agent, follow the [OSA source installation instructions](https://github.com/Miosa-osa/OSA#install-in-one-command) rather than assuming the installer supports it.
> An operating system appearing in registration does not guarantee desktop support for every architecture.

## 1. Install the agent on the machine

**Linux / macOS**

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Miosa-osa/OSA/main/scripts/install.sh -o /tmp/osa-install.sh
sh /tmp/osa-install.sh
osa version
```

If `osa` is not found, open a new shell and run `osa version` again.
Follow any platform-specific instructions printed by the installer.
For a pinned release, use the version-selection instructions in the [OSA installation guide](https://github.com/Miosa-osa/OSA#install-in-one-command).

**Windows**

Install the OSA agent from the release assets in the [OSA repository](https://github.com/Miosa-osa/OSA), then confirm the agent answers in a new terminal:

```powershell
osa version
```

Registration accepts `--platform windows`.
Desktop streaming depends on the agent build for your platform; a registered Windows or macOS host does not automatically have a working desktop.

## 2. Register the host and save its key

**miosa CLI**

```bash
miosa host register studio --platform linux
```

`--platform` takes `macos`, `linux`, or `windows`.
`register` creates the host record and prints the host ID and the host key once.
Add `--quiet-key` to print only the key, and `--region` to pin a region.

**MIOSA UI**

Open OpenComputers in MIOSA, choose **Connect a computer**, and register the machine in the intended organization.
Give it a recognizable name, such as `lab-server`, and select the operating system.
Save the returned host ID and one-time host key.

The **host key** authenticates this machine's agent.
Your **platform API key** authorizes REST requests from your terminal or backend.
They are different credentials and are not interchangeable.

## 3. Point the agent at MIOSA

On the machine itself, configure the connection with the OSA agent:

```bash
osa opencomputers login
osa opencomputers enable --no-profile
```

Paste the host key when prompted by `login`.
The prompt accepts the credential as terminal input; use a private terminal session.
Configuration is written under the agent user's `~/.osa` directory, including `open_computers.toml` and the `open_computers.ed25519` identity file.
Preserve that identity when updating the agent.

`login` saves the key and `enable` enables host mode.
Neither command proves that a live session has started.

## 4. Start the host session

Start the headless agent in the machine's terminal:

```bash
OSA_OPEN_COMPUTERS_ENABLED=true osa serve
```

Keep it running while completing the first check from another terminal.
The agent initiates an authenticated outbound WebSocket connection to MIOSA.
No inbound management port or public IP is required.

Open the host in MIOSA, or list it from your terminal, and confirm a fresh heartbeat and the capability needed for command execution:

```bash
miosa host list --tag studio
miosa host get <host>
```

If the host does not connect, follow [Host stays offline](/docs/opencomputers/troubleshooting#host-stays-offline).

## 5. Complete a command on the selected host

**miosa CLI**

```bash
miosa host jobs <host>
miosa host job list <host>
miosa host fs ls <host> --path /tmp
```

`miosa host jobs <host>` lists recent jobs. `miosa host job get <host> <job>` shows one job and its output.

**REST API**

In a separate trusted terminal, set your platform API key and the returned host ID:

```bash
export MIOSA_API_KEY="<your-platform-api-key>"
export HOST_ID="<your-host-id>"
```

Confirm the host record:

```bash
curl --fail-with-body -sS "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/opencomputers/hosts/$HOST_ID" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"
```

The response contains a `host` object.
Confirm its ID, name, heartbeat, and capabilities correspond to this machine.
Then run a read-only command:

```bash
curl --fail-with-body -sS \
  -X POST "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/opencomputers/hosts/$HOST_ID/exec" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"cmd":"hostname","stream":false,"timeout_ms":10000}'
```

Expected result, with your own job ID and hostname:

```json
{
  "job_id": "<job-id>",
  "exit_code": 0,
  "stdout": "lab-server\n",
  "stderr": ""
}
```

Compare `stdout` with `hostname` run directly on the machine.
With `stream: false` the API collects output; the default is `stream: true`, which returns SSE events until a terminal result.
For longer commands, use the [streaming exec contract](/docs/api-reference/open-computers#run-a-job) instead of this short collected-output check.

Use the IDs from your own request and the same authorized organization context.
An accepted request is not proof that the command completed.
Keep the API key in your backend or terminal environment.

## 6. Run the agent as a service

After the command passes, stop the foreground `osa serve` process before starting a second instance.

**Linux (systemd)**

The unit runs under the same user and home directory that hold the configured identity.
Run these commands as that user, not from a root login shell.
If this unit already exists, inspect it before replacing it; preserve any site-specific restrictions.

```bash
OSA_HOST_BIN="$(command -v osa)"
OSA_HOST_USER="$(id -un)"

sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/osa-opencomputers.service > /dev/null <<EOF_UNIT
[Unit]
Description=MIOSA OSA OpenComputers Host
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=${OSA_HOST_USER}
Environment=HOME=${HOME}
Environment=OSA_OPEN_COMPUTERS_ENABLED=true
ExecStart=${OSA_HOST_BIN} serve
Restart=always
RestartSec=5

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
EOF_UNIT

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now osa-opencomputers.service
systemctl status osa-opencomputers.service --no-pager
```

**Other service managers**

Use your platform's service manager under the same agent user, and keep two things with the service:

- the `OSA_OPEN_COMPUTERS_ENABLED=true` environment variable, so the agent starts in host mode;
- the `~/.osa` directory, including `open_computers.toml` and the `open_computers.ed25519` identity file.

A launch agent on macOS and a Windows service both work this way.
Then confirm a fresh heartbeat in MIOSA.

Expect an active service, then verify a new heartbeat in MIOSA and repeat the `hostname` request.
An enabled service should start at boot, but verify that behavior after a scheduled reboot before relying on unattended work.

## 7. Disconnect or retire the host

For temporary maintenance, stop dispatching new work, inspect running jobs, and stop the agent:

```bash
miosa host jobs <host>
sudo systemctl stop osa-opencomputers.service
```

The unit remains enabled for the next boot.
For retirement, disable startup, log the agent out, and revoke the host:

```bash
sudo systemctl disable --now osa-opencomputers.service
osa opencomputers logout
miosa host rm <host> --yes
```

Revocation and logout do not erase the machine's files, and they do not prove that every child process has stopped.
Verify active work before removing access or retrying it elsewhere.

- [Hosts and capabilities](/docs/opencomputers/hosts): Inspect a host and run work on one machine or a group.

- [OpenComputers troubleshooting](/docs/opencomputers/troubleshooting): Diagnose offline hosts, failed commands, identity rejection, and tunnels.
opencomputers/containers:
A host runs its own container runtime, and MIOSA manages containers on it: create, start, stop, restart, delete, and stream logs and resource usage.
Everything is addressed by the host ID and the container ID, and every operation is tenant-scoped.

MIOSA does not build the image for you. Your image must already be pullable by the host's runtime.

## Run a container

**miosa CLI**

```bash
miosa host container run <host> --image nginx:alpine --name web --set PORT=8080
miosa host container list <host>
miosa host container get <host> <container>
```

`miosa host container run` takes `--image`, `--name`, `--cmd` (repeatable), `--set KEY=VALUE` (repeatable), and `--restart`.
Aliases: `miosa host containers`, `miosa host container create`.

**REST API**

```bash
curl --fail-with-body -sS \
  -X POST "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/opencomputers/hosts/$HOST_ID/containers" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"web","image":"nginx:alpine","env":{"PORT":"8080"},"ports":[{"host_port":8080,"container_port":8080}]}'
```

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | Yes | 1 to 63 characters, starting with a letter or digit |
| `image` | string | Yes | Image reference the host's runtime can pull |
| `command` | string[] | No | Command and arguments; default `[]` (the image default) |
| `env` | object | No | Environment variables as a map; default `{}` |
| `ports` | object[] | No | `{host_port, container_port, protocol}`; `protocol` defaults to `tcp` |
| `volumes` | object[] | No | `{source, target, readonly}`; `readonly` defaults to `false` |
| `restart_policy` | string | No | `no`, `on-failure`, `always`, or `unless-stopped` (default) |
| `runtime` | string | No | `auto` (default), `docker`, or `podman` |

The response is `{"container": {...}}` with `id`, `name`, `image`, `command`, `env`, `ports`, `volumes`, `restart_policy`, `runtime`, `state`, `runtime_id`, `runtime_name`, `exit_code`, `started_at`, `stopped_at`, `last_error`, `last_cpu_percent`, `last_mem_mb`, and `last_stats_at`.

Container states are `provisioning`, `running`, `stopped`, `failed`, `removing`, and `removed`.

> **Note: Check state, do not assume it**
>
> `create` returns as soon as the host accepts the request. Read `state` before you rely on the container: `provisioning` is not `running`, and `last_error` is where a failed start explains itself.

## Logs

**miosa CLI**

```bash
miosa host container logs <host> <container>
miosa host container logs <host> <container> --json
```

Streams until the connection ends or you press Ctrl-C. With `--json`, each event is one JSON object per line.

**REST API**

```bash
curl -N --fail-with-body -sS \
  "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/opencomputers/hosts/$HOST_ID/containers/$CONTAINER_ID/logs" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"
```

An SSE stream of `{stream, line, ts}` frames, where `stream` is the source stream on the container.

## Stats

**miosa CLI**

```bash
miosa host container stats <host> <container>
miosa host container stats <host> <container> --json
```

**REST API**

```bash
curl -N --fail-with-body -sS \
  "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/opencomputers/hosts/$HOST_ID/containers/$CONTAINER_ID/stats" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"
```

An SSE stream that ticks about every 10 seconds with `{container_id, cpu_percent, mem_mb, stats_at}`, and sends a final `{state, container_id}` frame when the container stops.

The latest sample is also kept on the container record as `last_cpu_percent`, `last_mem_mb`, and `last_stats_at`.

## Lifecycle

```bash
miosa host container start <host> <container>
miosa host container stop <host> <container>
miosa host container restart <host> <container>
miosa host container rm <host> <container> --force --yes
```

| Action | REST | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Start | `POST /opencomputers/hosts/{host_id}/containers/{id}/start` | Only from `stopped` or `failed`; returns `409` otherwise |
| Stop | `POST .../containers/{id}/stop` | Only from `running`; accepts a `timeout_s` grace period, default 10 |
| Restart | `POST .../containers/{id}/restart` | Allowed from `running`, `stopped`, or `failed` |
| Update | `PATCH .../containers/{id}` | `image`, `command`, `env`, `ports`, `volumes`, `restart_policy`, `runtime` |
| Delete | `DELETE .../containers/{id}?force=true` | `force` deletes a running container; returns `202` |

Deleting a container does not delete its volumes for you unless you asked for the volume to be removed with the container.

## Compose projects

A compose project is a docker-compose file the host keeps running.

```bash
miosa host compose list <host>
miosa host compose up <host> app --build --pull
miosa host compose down <host> app --remove-volumes
miosa host compose rm <host> app --yes
```

| Action | REST |
|---|---|
| List | `GET /opencomputers/hosts/{host_id}/compose-projects` |
| Create | `POST .../compose-projects` with `name`, `yaml` (required), `env`, `pull`, `build` |
| Up | `POST .../compose-projects/{id}/up` |
| Down | `POST .../compose-projects/{id}/down` with `remove_volumes` |
| Delete | `DELETE .../compose-projects/{id}` |
| Events | `GET .../compose-projects/{id}/events` (SSE) |

Compose project states are `creating`, `running`, `partial`, `stopped`, `failed`, and `removing`.
The events stream carries `{type, payload}` frames where `type` is `progress`, `log`, or `error`.

`--remove-volumes` destroys the project's volumes. Confirm what you intend to lose before using it on a stateful project.

## Plan limits

The number of container slots a tenant can use depends on the plan, and a compose project counts its services against the same budget.

| Plan | Containers and compose service slots |
|---|---|
| `free` | 2 |
| `starter` | 10 |
| `pro` | 50 |
| `team` | 250 |
| `enterprise` | 1000 |

Exceeding the limit returns `402` with `error: "plan_limit_reached"`, plus the `limit` and `current` values.
See [Billing and limits](/docs/opencomputers/billing) for the other plan-scoped limits.

> **Caution: A container on a host is not a sandbox**
>
> Containers share the host's kernel. They are not Firecracker microVMs, and they do not give you the isolation or the disposable lifecycle of a [sandbox](/docs/develop/sandboxes).
> Use containers when you want a long-lived service on a machine you own.
opencomputers/devices:
A device is any runtime MIOSA can run a command on.
`<device>` is an id, not a name, and the device surface does not care which kind of runtime answers.

Use it when a script has to work across runtime kinds, or when you have an id and do not know what it is.

> **Note: Devices and hosts are different surfaces**
>
> The `/api/v1/devices` endpoints resolve sandbox workers and managed Computers - the runtimes MIOSA provisions for you.
> A machine you connect with OpenComputers is a **host** and is addressed by its host ID through the [OpenComputers endpoints](/docs/api-reference/open-computers) instead.
> The [`miosa device`](/docs/cli/devices) command is the CLI's unified view; for a host, use the typed [`miosa host`](/docs/cli/platform#your-own-hosts) family.

## List and inspect

**miosa CLI**

```bash
miosa device list
miosa device list --status running --name web --limit 20
miosa device get <device>
miosa device capabilities <device>
```

Aliases: `miosa devices`, `show` for `get`, `caps` for `capabilities`.

**REST API**

```bash
curl --fail-with-body -sS "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/devices?status=running" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"

curl --fail-with-body -sS "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/devices/$DEVICE_ID/capabilities" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"
```

`GET /api/v1/devices` accepts `status`, `name`, and `limit` (default 50).

A device record carries `id`, `name`, `slug`, `template`, `kind`, `state`, `ip_address`, `node_id`, `running`, `terminal`, and its `capabilities`.

## Check capabilities before you act

Capabilities are the difference between a script that works everywhere and one that fails on half your devices.

| Capability | Sandbox worker | Computer |
|---|---|---|
| `exec` | yes | yes |
| `files` | yes | yes |
| `browser` | no | yes |
| `artifacts` | yes | no |
| `live_server` | yes | yes |
| `connectors` | yes | yes |
| `pause`, `resume` | yes | yes |
| `snapshots` | yes | no |

Read the capability rather than assuming it from the device's name.

## Run a command

**miosa CLI**

```bash
miosa device exec <device> -- uname -a
miosa device exec <device> -c "npm test" --timeout-ms 120000
```

`miosa device exec` exits with the remote command's status, like `miosa exec`.

**REST API**

```bash
curl --fail-with-body -sS \
  -X POST "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/devices/$DEVICE_ID/exec" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"command":"uname -a","timeout_ms":30000}'
```

The body takes `command` (required) and `timeout_ms` or `timeout` in seconds (default 30).

Exec on a device resolves a **running** target.
A device that is not running returns `DEVICE_NOT_RUNNING` with the current `state` rather than starting it for you.

## Files

**miosa CLI**

```bash
miosa device files <device> --path /workspace
miosa device read <device> --path /workspace/out.json
miosa device write <device> --path /workspace/app.py --content "print(1)"
```

Aliases: `ls` for `files`.

**REST API**

```bash
curl --fail-with-body -sS "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/devices/$DEVICE_ID/files?path=/workspace" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"

curl --fail-with-body -sS "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/devices/$DEVICE_ID/files/read?path=/workspace/out.json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"

curl --fail-with-body -sS \
  -X POST "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/devices/$DEVICE_ID/files/write" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"path":"/workspace/app.py","content":"print(1)"}'
```

`files` lists a directory and defaults to `/workspace`. `files/read` takes a required `path` and returns the content base64-encoded with `encoding: "base64"`. `files/write` takes `path` plus either `content_base64` or `content`.

`miosa device read` returns the file contents base64-encoded, and `miosa device write` takes the contents from `--content` or a JSON body with `--file`.

## Expose a port

```bash
miosa device expose <device> 3000

curl --fail-with-body -sS \
  -X POST "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/devices/$DEVICE_ID/expose" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"port":3000}'
```

On a host, the typed [tunnel commands](/docs/opencomputers/tunnels) give you the fuller surface: access mode, slug control, and list and delete.

## Browser URL

```bash
miosa device browser <device>
```

`GET /api/v1/devices/{id}/browser` returns the streamed desktop for a computer, with `desktop_url`, `ws_url`, `token`, `expires_at`, `computer_id`, and `slug`, and a one-hour token TTL.
A sandbox returns `BROWSER_UNSUPPORTED_FOR_SANDBOX`; use a [Computer](/docs/computer-use) when you need a desktop.

## Lifecycle

```bash
miosa device extend <device> --timeout 2h
miosa device pause <device>
miosa device resume <device>
miosa device stop <device>
miosa device rm <device> --yes
```

| Action | REST | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Extend | `POST /devices/{id}/extend` with `timeout_sec` | Replaces the time to live |
| Pause | `POST /devices/{id}/pause` | Keeps the disk |
| Resume | `POST /devices/{id}/resume` | |
| Stop | `POST /devices/{id}/stop` | Keeps the disk |
| Destroy | `DELETE /devices/{id}` | Permanent; returns state `destroyed` |

Each lifecycle call returns the device's new `state`.

## Error codes

| Code | Status | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `MISSING_PARAM` | 400 | A required field is absent; the response names it |
| `INVALID_PARAM` | 400 | A field is present but not usable |
| `INVALID_BASE64` | 400 | File content was not valid base64 |
| `NOT_FOUND` | 404 | The device does not exist, or is not yours |
| `DEVICE_NOT_RUNNING` | 409 | The device is not running; the response carries its `state` |
| `UNSUPPORTED_FOR_COMPUTER` | 422 | The operation does not apply to a computer |
| `BROWSER_UNSUPPORTED_FOR_SANDBOX` | 422 | Browsing requires a computer |
| `DEVICE_OPERATION_FAILED` | 422 | The runtime rejected the operation |

- [Computers](/docs/computers/overview): The managed desktop runtime behind computer devices.
opencomputers/gha-runners:
A runner is a GitHub Actions runner the host keeps registered for one repository.
MIOSA installs and supervises the runner process on your machine, so a workflow job runs on hardware you control.

Use this when a build needs a GPU, a large local cache, software that only exists on your machine, or a network path that GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach.

## Register a runner

**miosa CLI**

```bash
miosa host gha-runner list <host>
miosa host gha-runner new <host> --repo https://github.com/acme/app --token <token>
miosa host gha-runner new <host> --repo https://github.com/acme/app --token-secret GH_TOKEN --ephemeral
miosa host gha-runner get <host> <runner>
```

Aliases: `miosa host gha-runners`, `miosa host runner`, `miosa host runners`, and `create` or `add` for `new`.

**REST API**

```bash
curl --fail-with-body -sS \
  -X POST "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/opencomputers/hosts/$HOST_ID/gha-runners" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"repo_url":"https://github.com/acme/app","name":"gpu-builder","labels":["gpu","linux"],"pat_secret_id":"<secret-id>"}'
```

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `repo_url` | string | Yes | Repository URL; must be on `github.com` or a `*.github.com` host |
| `name` | string | Yes | Runner name, 1 to 128 characters; unique per host |
| `labels` | string[] | No | Runner labels; default `[]` |
| `ephemeral` | boolean | No | Deregister the runner after one job; default `false` |
| `pat_secret_id` | string | One of | ID of an existing host secret holding a GitHub token |
| `pat_value` | string | One of | Inline token; MIOSA stores it as a host secret for you |

The CLI flag names differ from the API field names: `--repo` maps to `repo_url`, `--token` to `pat_value` (sent to the host and not stored), and `--token-secret` to `pat_secret_id`.
`--label` is repeatable, and `--name` defaults to a generated name.

> **Caution: MIOSA never returns the token**
>
> The GitHub token is not stored in a readable form and is never returned by any read.
> Prefer `pat_secret_id` or `--token-secret` so the value lives in a [host secret](/docs/opencomputers/hosts#secrets) rather than in a command you might paste elsewhere.

> **Note: GitHub Enterprise Server is not supported**
>
> `repo_url` must point at `github.com`. A GHES URL is rejected with a `422`.

## Runner states

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `provisioning` | MIOSA is installing and starting the runner |
| `idle` | Registered and waiting for a job |
| `running_job` | Executing a workflow job |
| `offline` | Registered but not reachable |
| `failed` | Installation or registration failed |
| `removed` | Deregistered |

`current_job` is set while the runner is executing, and `last_activity_at` tells you when it last did anything.

## Watch a runner

**miosa CLI**

```bash
miosa host gha-runner events <host> <runner>
miosa host gha-runner events <host> <runner> --json
```

Streams events as the runner picks up and finishes jobs. Ctrl-C stops the stream.

**REST API**

```bash
curl -N --fail-with-body -sS \
  "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/opencomputers/hosts/$HOST_ID/gha-runners/$RUNNER_ID/events" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"
```

Named SSE events: `progress`, `ready`, `status`, `error`, and `removed`.

## Repair and remove

```bash
miosa host gha-runner refresh <host> <runner>
miosa host gha-runner rm <host> <runner> --yes
```

| Action | REST | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Refresh | `POST .../gha-runners/{runner_id}/refresh` | Reinstalls and restarts the runner; returns `{"ok": true}` |
| Remove | `DELETE .../gha-runners/{runner_id}` | Stops the runner and deregisters it from GitHub; returns `204` |

`refresh` is the fix for a runner stuck in `failed` or `offline` after an upgrade, rather than deleting and re-registering.
Both actions can return `429` if the GitHub API rate-limits the registration calls.

## Reference it in a workflow

Point a workflow job at the runner's labels:

```yaml
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: [self-hosted, gpu, linux]
```

A job runs on your machine only while the host agent is connected and the runner is `idle`.
If the host goes offline mid-job, the workflow fails on GitHub's side; check `miosa host gha-runner get` and the [runner events](/docs/opencomputers/gha-runners#watch-a-runner) before retrying.
opencomputers/hosts:
A host is one enrolled machine.
Every host is addressed by its host ID, and every host command takes `<host>` as its first argument.
The host ID is stable; the machine's IP address and hostname are not the identity MIOSA uses.

```bash
miosa host list --tag studio
miosa host get <host>
```

`miosa host list` takes `--tag` to narrow to hosts carrying a tag.
`miosa host get <host>` returns the host record with its platform, region, tags, and reported capabilities.
Aliases: `miosa hosts`, `miosa host`.

## What a host reports

| Command | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| `miosa host get <host>` | The host record: state, platform, region, tags, capabilities |
| `miosa host metrics <host>` | CPU, memory, and disk of the host |
| `miosa host runtime <host>` | The container runtime the host is running |
| `miosa host services <host>` | The services running on the host |
| `miosa host jobs <host>` | Recent commands dispatched to the host |

Registration alone proves neither readiness nor feature parity.
Treat a fresh heartbeat plus a completed operation as the evidence that a host is usable for the capability you need.

> **Caution: Check the capability, not the interface**
>
> A common MIOSA interface does not mean every host supports every managed operation.
> Direct execution runs within the host user's operating-system permissions; it does not automatically place each command in an isolated microVM.
> Registration does not turn an arbitrary host into a sandbox worker pool or an Docker Host host.

## Run a command

Commands dispatched to a host are jobs.

```bash
miosa host job list <host>
miosa host job get <host> <job>
miosa host job cancel <host> <job>
```

`miosa host job` has aliases `jobs` and `exec`, so `miosa host exec <host> -- uname -a` is the same surface.
Cancelling a job is not proof that the remote process stopped; confirm the outcome before retrying work with side effects.

The REST equivalent is the [exec endpoint](/docs/api-reference/open-computers#run-a-job), which streams SSE by default and returns collected output when you send `"stream": false`.

### Run on every host in a group

A group is a named set of hosts. Running a command or installing an app on a group runs it on every member.

```bash
miosa host group new ci --description "CI workers"
miosa host group add ci <host>
miosa host group exec ci --cmd npm --arg test --cwd /srv/app --timeout-ms 120000
miosa host group get ci
miosa host group remove ci <host>
miosa host group rm ci --yes
```

Deleting a group leaves its hosts in place.

## Files on a host

Paths are on the host's own file system, not a sandbox workspace.

```bash
miosa host fs ls <host> --path /srv/app
miosa host fs stat <host> --path /srv/app/package.json
miosa host fs mkdir <host> --path /srv/app/logs
miosa host fs rm <host> --path /srv/app/old.log --yes
```

`miosa host fs ls` defaults to the agent user's home directory.
The same operations are available over REST under `/opencomputers/hosts/{id}/fs/*` - see the [OpenComputers API](/docs/api-reference/open-computers#file-system).

## Tags

Tags group hosts for selection and batch work.

```bash
miosa host tag add <host> gpu
miosa host tag list
miosa host tag rm <host> gpu
```

`miosa host list --tag gpu` then selects hosts without you tracking IDs by hand.

## Secrets

Host secrets are encrypted key-value pairs that the host agent can use at runtime.
Values are never returned by a list call.

```bash
miosa host secret list <host>
miosa host secret set <host> GITHUB_TOKEN --description "CI token"
miosa host secret set <host> DEPLOY_KEY --key-stdin < deploy.key
miosa host secret rm <host> GITHUB_TOKEN --yes
```

`secret set` prompts for the value or reads it from standard input with `--key-stdin`, so the value does not land in your shell history.

## SSH keys

Only public keys are handled.

```bash
miosa host ssh-key add <host> --name roberto --public-key "ssh-ed25519 AAAA..."
miosa host ssh-key import <host> <github-user>
miosa host ssh-key list <host>
miosa host ssh-key rm <host> <key> --yes
```

`ssh-key import` copies the public keys a GitHub user has published.

## Apps

The catalog lists what MIOSA can install; install puts one on a host.

```bash
miosa host app catalog
miosa host app install <host> redis
miosa host app list <host>
miosa host app health <host> redis
miosa host app start <host> redis
miosa host app uninstall <host> redis --yes
```

Check `miosa host app health` after an install rather than assuming the app came up.

## Compose projects

A compose project is a docker-compose file the host keeps running.

```bash
miosa host compose list <host>
miosa host compose up <host> app --build --pull
miosa host compose down <host> app --remove-volumes
miosa host compose rm <host> app --yes
```

`--build` builds images first and `--pull` pulls them first.
`--remove-volumes` deletes the project's volumes, so confirm what you intend to lose before using it on a stateful project.

## Containers

Containers on a host are covered in [Containers](/docs/opencomputers/containers).

## Clusters

A cluster is a group of your hosts that serve one model together, exposed as an OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

```bash
miosa host cluster list
miosa host cluster get <cluster>
miosa host cluster start <cluster>
miosa host cluster stop <cluster>
miosa host cluster rm <cluster> --yes
```

Clusters are created over the API with `host_ids`, `name`, and `model`; see [Inference clusters](/docs/api-reference/open-computers#inference-clusters).

## Remove a host

```bash
miosa host rm <host> --yes
```

Removing a host ends its ability to authenticate.
It does not erase the machine's files and does not prove that its processes stopped.

- [OpenComputers API](/docs/api-reference/open-computers): Hosts, jobs, files, tunnels, agents, clusters, and secrets over REST.
opencomputers/meshes:
A mesh is a named private network across several of your hosts.
MIOSA assigns each member an address in the mesh's `/24` and distributes WireGuard keys, so members reach each other directly without exposing anything on the public internet.

Use a mesh when services on one host need to talk to services on another: a database on one box, an application on a second, a GPU worker on a third.

## Create a mesh

**miosa CLI**

```bash
miosa host mesh list
miosa host mesh new lab --host <host> --host <host>
miosa host mesh get lab
```

Aliases: `miosa host meshes`.

**REST API**

```bash
curl --fail-with-body -sS \
  -X POST "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/opencomputers/meshes" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"lab","host_ids":["<host-1>","<host-2>"]}'
```

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | Yes | 1 to 80 lowercase alphanumeric or hyphen characters |
| `host_ids` | string[] | No | Hosts to add at creation; default `[]` |

A mesh carries a `cidr` in the form `10.x.x.0/24`, a `state`, and a `listen_port_base` that defaults to `51820`.
Mesh states are `provisioning`, `active`, `failed`, and `torn_down`.

## Manage membership

```bash
miosa host mesh add-host lab <host>
miosa host mesh remove-host lab <host> --yes
miosa host mesh rm lab --yes
```

| Action | REST |
|---|---|
| Add a host | `POST /opencomputers/meshes/{id}/hosts/{host_id}` |
| Remove a host | `DELETE /opencomputers/meshes/{id}/hosts/{host_id}` |
| Delete the mesh | `DELETE /opencomputers/meshes/{id}` |

Adding a host returns the new peer.
Removing a host leaves the host itself in place; deleting the mesh tears down the WireGuard configuration before the record is removed.

> **Note: A mesh caps at 253 hosts**
>
> The mesh's `/24` address space allows 253 members. Adding one past that returns `422` with `mesh /24 is full (max 253 hosts)`.
> If you outgrow a single mesh, contact support rather than nesting meshes yourself.

## Inspect peers

`miosa host mesh get <mesh>` and `GET /opencomputers/meshes/{id}` return the mesh with its current peer list.

| Peer field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `id` | Peer record ID |
| `host_id` | The host this peer represents |
| `assigned_ip` | Address in the mesh's `10.x.x.x` range |
| `pubkey` | The peer's WireGuard public key |
| `endpoint` | Last seen endpoint |
| `latest_handshake` | When the tunnel last completed a handshake |
| `rx_bytes`, `tx_bytes` | Traffic counters |
| `state` | `pending_key`, `configured`, `active`, or `failed` |

Peer states are the fastest way to answer "is this host actually reachable over the mesh": an `active` peer with a recent `latest_handshake` is, and a `pending_key` peer never joined.

## Events

**miosa CLI**

```bash
miosa host mesh events lab
```

Streams host joins, key rotation, and state changes until you press Ctrl-C.

**REST API**

```bash
curl -N --fail-with-body -sS \
  "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/opencomputers/meshes/$MESH_ID/events" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"
```

Named SSE events: `mesh_peer_active`, `mesh_peer_down`, and `mesh_status`.

## Security notes

- Mesh traffic is encrypted and stays inside the mesh. It does not become reachable from the internet because a host is a member.
- MIOSA distributes the WireGuard keys. An operator with control-plane access can add a host to a mesh, so treat mesh membership as a privileged change and review it in the [audit log](/docs/opencomputers/security#audit-log).
- A mesh does not grant a host access to anything else on another host beyond the ports that host's firewall and services allow.

opencomputers/security:
OpenComputers inverts the usual direction of a management connection. The agent on your machine dials out to MIOSA; MIOSA never dials in. That single design decision determines most of what is and is not possible here. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Prem["Your machine"] Agent["MIOSA host agent"] User["Agent OS user"] Local["Files and services
reachable by that user"] Agent --> User User --> Local end Agent -->|"Outbound authenticated WebSocket :443"| CP["MIOSA control plane"] CP -->|"Authorized operation"| Agent CP -->|"Nothing inbound"| X["No inbound port,
no public IP required"] ``` ## What MIOSA can do - Send an authorized operation over the session the agent already opened: a command, a file read or write, a container action, a backup, or a tunnel dial. - Read the host's reported state: platform, architecture, capabilities, runtime, tags, heartbeat, agent version, and job history. - Route an inbound HTTP request down an existing session, but only through a [tunnel you created](/docs/opencomputers/tunnels) and only if the request satisfies that tunnel's access mode. ## What MIOSA cannot do - Open a connection to your machine spontaneously. There is no inbound management port and no requirement for a public IP. - Act with more privilege than the agent's own operating-system user. Direct execution runs as that user, with that user's filesystem permissions and network reach. - See files the agent user cannot read, or services that user cannot reach. - Replace your operating-system controls. The agent is not a sandbox, a hypervisor, or a jail. > **Caution: Direct host execution is not isolated** > > Running a command on a host executes it in the host's own environment, not in an isolated microVM. > Registration alone does not make a host a sandbox worker pool or an Docker Host host. > If you need isolation, put the work in a [sandbox](/docs/develop/sandboxes) instead of on a host. ## Credentials Two credentials exist, they have different jobs, and they are not interchangeable. | Credential | Who uses it | Lifetime | |---|---|---| | **Host key** | The agent on the machine, from `osa opencomputers login` | Returned once at registration; revocable | | **Platform API key** | Your terminal, backend, or SDK | Managed in [API keys](/docs/platform/api-keys) | The host also keeps an Ed25519 identity file, `~/.osa/open_computers.ed25519`, which pins the machine's identity. Preserve that file across agent upgrades. If it is lost, revoke the host and register a new one rather than copying another machine's identity or disabling verification. You can check whether a host key is still valid without touching the host: ```bash curl --fail-with-body -sS \ -X POST "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/opencomputers/hosts/registration-status" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"host_key":""}' ``` It answers `{connected, state, host}`, with `410` for a revoked key and `401` for an invalid one. ## Authorization Operations are authorized at the control plane, and every record is tenant-scoped. - Commands dispatched to a host require the `opencomputers:write` scope. - Host runtime registration, enrollment, and certification use `cloud:read` and `cloud:write`. - Host listing, files, containers, tunnels, meshes, backups, and secrets rely on the API pipeline's organization authorization and workspace membership, and each handler resolves the resource through a tenant-scoped lookup. A host ID from another organization resolves to nothing, not to someone else's machine. ## Secrets Host and tenant secrets are encrypted key-value pairs. List calls return names, descriptions, and IDs, never values. ```bash miosa host secret set GITHUB_TOKEN --key-stdin < token.txt miosa host secret list ``` The REST reveal endpoint, `POST /api/v1/opencomputers/hosts/{id}/secrets/{secret_id}/reveal`, is the only way to read a value back, and every call is audit-logged. ## Audit log Every authorization-relevant action lands in the OpenComputers audit log. ```bash curl --fail-with-body -sS "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/opencomputers/audit?limit=50" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" ``` | Endpoint | What it does | |---|---| | `GET /opencomputers/audit` | Cursor-paginated events; filter by `kind`, `host_id`, `actor`, `from`, and `to` | | `GET /opencomputers/audit/export` | The same data as JSON or CSV, up to 5000 rows | | `GET /opencomputers/audit/verify` | Verifies the integrity chain and reports the last good index | | `GET /opencomputers/audit/:id` | One event | | `GET /opencomputers/audit/live` | A live SSE feed | Run `verify` on a schedule: it answers whether the stored audit history is intact, which is what makes the log useful after an incident. ## Webhooks OpenComputers webhooks POST events to your endpoint with an HMAC-SHA256 signature over the raw body, under a signing secret returned once when the webhook is created. ```bash curl --fail-with-body -sS -X POST "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/opencomputers/webhooks" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"name":"host-alerts","url":"https://example.com/hooks/miosa","events":["host.disconnected"]}' ``` Verify the signature over the exact bytes you received, before you parse them. `GET .../webhooks/{id}/deliveries` shows recent attempts, and `POST .../webhooks/{id}/test` sends one on demand. See [Webhooks](/docs/integrations/webhooks) for the general delivery contract. ## Data boundaries Executing on your machine keeps the execution on your machine. It does not mean every byte stays there. | Data | Where it travels | |---|---| | The command and its arguments | Sent over the session; the command is recorded in audit | | Command output and file contents you request | Returned through MIOSA as part of the workflow | | Backup chunks | Uploaded to MIOSA storage, encrypted at rest | | Desktop and terminal streams | Routed through MIOSA while a session is open | | Model requests from an agent run | Sent to the model endpoint you configured, which may be a third party | Set the agent's permissions, the tunnel access modes, and the model endpoints to match the data you are willing to move. For a fuller treatment of hardware ownership and connectivity, see [Shared responsibility](/docs/infrastructure/shared-responsibility). ## Revocation and teardown ```bash miosa host rm --yes ``` Revoking a host ends its ability to authenticate immediately. It does not erase the machine's files, and it does not stop a process already running there. Before you revoke or retire a host, stop new work, inspect its [jobs](/docs/opencomputers/hosts#run-a-command), and confirm the outcome of anything in flight. - [Connect your first host](/docs/opencomputers/connect): Install, enroll, and verify a machine. - [Shared responsibility](/docs/infrastructure/shared-responsibility): Who operates the hardware, operating system, network, and control plane.
opencomputers/troubleshooting:
Start with the exact host ID, organization, and operation that failed.
Check both the control-plane record and the machine itself.
A working login, a healthy API endpoint, or a saved host key is not proof that the host can execute your request.

The fastest first check is always the same:

```bash
miosa host get <host>
miosa host jobs <host>
```

`state` and `connected` describe now; the job list describes what actually happened.

## Host stays offline

1. Confirm the machine is awake and its network connection works.
2. Check the agent process on the host; for the systemd setup in [Connect your first host](/docs/opencomputers/connect), use the commands below.
3. Check outbound HTTPS and WebSocket access to `api.miosa.ai` on port 443; an HTTP health check alone does not test WebSocket proxying.
4. Confirm the service runs as the user whose `~/.osa/open_computers.toml` contains the intended host configuration.
5. Check that the host has not been revoked, then confirm a fresh heartbeat in MIOSA.

```bash
systemctl status osa-opencomputers.service --no-pager
journalctl -u osa-opencomputers.service -n 50 --no-pager
```

Use `sudo` for logs if your account cannot read the system journal.
`osa opencomputers status` can help inspect configuration, but its session output describes the runtime queried by that command.
Confirm the actual service and control-plane heartbeat before concluding that a separate background process is offline.

## Key saved but no connection

`osa opencomputers login` saves a host key, and `connect` is an alias for that command.
The agent still has to start in host mode; saving the credential alone does not start the session.
Follow the [startup steps](/docs/opencomputers/connect#4-start-the-host-session).
Do not substitute a platform API key for the host key.

## Identity rejected after reinstall

The machine's identity file must match the identity pinned when the host first connected.
Preserve `~/.osa/open_computers.ed25519`, along with the host configuration, during upgrades.
If the identity is lost, revoke the host and register a new one rather than copying another machine's identity or disabling verification.

## Registration fails

| Error | Cause |
|---|---|
| `402 plan_limit_reached` | Your plan's host limit is reached; the response carries `limit` and `current` |
| `422 name is required` | `name` is missing, empty, or over 64 characters |
| `501 open_computers_disabled` | OpenComputers is not enabled for this environment |

Check the plan's host allowance in [Billing and limits](/docs/opencomputers/billing) before assuming a bug.

## Command fails or appears stuck

| Symptom | What to check |
|---|---|
| `cmd is required` | Send the `cmd` field to the exec endpoint; `command` is the field name on the newer `POST .../jobs` route, not on `/exec` |
| `409 host_not_connected` | The host is offline. Bring the agent up before dispatching |
| `422 invalid_command` | The command is empty or over 8192 characters |
| `422 invalid_args` | More than 256 arguments, or a non-string argument |
| `422 invalid_timeout` | The timeout is outside 1 to 3600 seconds |
| `502 dispatch_failed` | The session dropped while dispatching; check the agent, then retry once |

- **Permission denied or command unavailable:** run the same command locally as the agent user and check its permissions, working directory, PATH, and supported operations.
- **HTTP request remains open:** exec streams by default; inspect SSE events until `exec_result` or `exec_error`, or use `stream: false` for a short command.
- **Timeout or connection loss:** save the returned job ID, inspect the job and the local process, and establish the outcome before retrying.

```bash
curl --fail-with-body -sS \
  "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/opencomputers/hosts/$HOST_ID/exec/$JOB_ID" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"
```

A timeout or a disconnected client is not proof that the process stopped.
Avoid retrying a deployment, payment, file mutation, or other operation with side effects merely because the client disconnected.

## Containers

| Symptom | What to check |
|---|---|
| `503 host_not_connected` | The container runtime is managed by the agent on the host; an offline host cannot create or start containers |
| `402 plan_limit_reached` | The container and compose slot budget is full; see [Billing and limits](/docs/opencomputers/billing) |
| Stuck in `provisioning` | The host is pulling the image, or the image reference is not pullable by that host's runtime |
| `409` on start | A container only starts from `stopped` or `failed`; check `state` first |
| `last_error` set | The runtime rejected the container; read `last_error` before retrying |

Pulling a large image over a slow link can take minutes. Watch the host's disk and network with `miosa host metrics <host>` rather than recreating the container.

## Meshes

| Symptom | What to check |
|---|---|
| Peer stuck in `pending_key` | The host has not completed its key exchange; confirm the host is online and the agent is current |
| Peer `active` but traffic fails | The services on the other host may not be listening on the address you dialed, or a host firewall blocks the mesh interface |
| `422 mesh /24 is full` | The mesh has reached 253 members |
| `422 one or more hosts not found` | A host ID belongs to another organization or does not exist |

Use `miosa host mesh get <mesh>` and read `latest_handshake`, `rx_bytes`, and `tx_bytes` to tell "never connected" from "connected but no traffic".

## GitHub Actions runners

| Symptom | What to check |
|---|---|
| `422 GitHub API rejected the PAT` | The token lacks repository or organization runner permissions, or has expired |
| `422 GitHub repo/org not found` | The `repo_url` is wrong, or the token cannot see it. GitHub Enterprise Server URLs are not supported |
| `429 GitHub API rate limit exceeded` | GitHub throttled the registration call; wait and retry |
| Runner `offline` | The host is offline, or the runner process died. Use `miosa host gha-runner refresh <host> <runner>` |
| Runner `failed` | Read the runner events; a failed install is usually a missing dependency on the host |

A workflow that never schedules is usually a label mismatch: check that the workflow's `runs-on` labels match the runner's `labels`.

## Backups

| Symptom | What to check |
|---|---|
| `503` on trigger | The source host must be connected to take a snapshot |
| Snapshot `failed` | Read `error` on the snapshot; a path that disappeared or a permission change are the common causes |
| `422 snapshot has no chunks` | The snapshot did not complete; only `complete` snapshots restore |
| `503 target host not connected` | Restores are pushed by the target host's agent, so the target must be online |
| `403 cross-organization restore not allowed` | The target host is not in the same organization as the snapshot |

## Tunnel does not reach the application

1. On the host, confirm the application is running and responds on the intended local port.
2. Check the tunnel's configured `target_port` and the host's connection.
3. Open the returned `public_url`; do not construct a hostname yourself.
4. Confirm the viewer meets the tunnel's access policy.

| Proxy error | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `connection_refused` | Nothing is listening on `target_port` on the host |
| `target_port_not_allowed` | The port is outside the range the host agent permits |
| `tunnels_disabled_on_host` | Tunnels are disabled on that host |
| `too_many_concurrent_tunnels` | The host is at its concurrent tunnel limit |
| `502 host_offline` | The host dropped while the request was in flight |
| `503 tunnel paused` | The tunnel is in state `paused` |
| `401` with `WWW-Authenticate: Basic` | The tunnel is in `password` mode and the request did not carry credentials |

A public URL cannot make an unavailable local service healthy.
Do not change a private tunnel to public solely to troubleshoot authentication.

## Commands work but desktop does not

A headless host can execute commands without providing a desktop.
Verify the selected host advertises desktop support and has the required session and streaming backend.
Check the agent's current platform support; registering macOS or Windows does not guarantee a working desktop stream.
For a MIOSA-managed Computer, follow [desktop readiness](/docs/computers/fast-start) instead of installing a desktop on an arbitrary host.

## Customer-cloud resources exist but placement is unavailable

Cloud infrastructure existing is only one onboarding step.
Verify provider acceptance, a successful live canary, and host readiness before expecting placement.
See the [BYOC overview](/docs/infrastructure/byoc/overview) for the applicable gates.

## Information to include when asking for help

Include the host ID, the operation or job ID, a timestamp with timezone, the agent version, the OS and architecture, and the relevant error text.
State whether the command works locally as the agent user and whether the heartbeat is fresh.
Remove API keys, host keys, identity files, private URLs containing tokens, and sensitive command output from shared logs.

- [Connect your first host](/docs/opencomputers/connect): Repeat the connection and completed-command checks.

- [Billing and limits](/docs/opencomputers/billing): Check plan limits before treating a 402 as a fault.
opencomputers/tunnels:
A tunnel publishes a port on one of your hosts at a MIOSA-managed address.
The host keeps dialing out to MIOSA; MIOSA routes inbound requests back down that session to your service.

An outbound management session and a publicly reachable application tunnel are different things.
Connecting a host does not expose anything. A tunnel is an explicit, separate exposure with its own access policy.

## Create a tunnel

```bash
miosa host tunnel new <host> --port 3000 --slug my-app-dev --access organization
miosa host tunnel list <host>
miosa host tunnel get <host> <tunnel>
miosa host tunnel rm <host> <tunnel> --yes
```

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--port int` | Port on the host to expose |
| `--slug string` | Address name (default: generated) |
| `--access string` | Who may open it: `organization` (default) or `public` |

The same call over REST:

```bash
curl --fail-with-body -sS \
  -X POST "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/opencomputers/hosts/$HOST_ID/tunnels" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"target_port":3000,"auth_mode":"tenant_only","slug":"my-app-dev"}'
```

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `target_port` | integer | Yes | Local port to expose, `1` to `65535` |
| `auth_mode` | string | No | `public` \| `tenant_only` \| `password` (default: `tenant_only`) |
| `slug` | string | No | Address name, 4 to 63 lowercase alphanumeric or hyphen characters |
| `target_host` | string | No | Host to dial from the agent (default: `127.0.0.1`) |
| `password` | string | No | Required in practice when `auth_mode` is `password`; hashed, never returned |

```json
{
  "id": "tun_abc",
  "host_id": "host_abc123",
  "slug": "my-app-dev",
  "target_port": 3000,
  "auth_mode": "tenant_only",
  "public_url": "https://<public-host>/t/my-app-dev",
  "enabled": true,
  "created_at": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z",
  "updated_at": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"
}
```

Use the returned `public_url`. Do not construct a hostname yourself: the routing domain is set per environment, so read it from the response instead of hardcoding one.

## Change or disable a tunnel

```bash
miosa host tunnel new <host> --port 8080 --slug my-app-dev   # re-create with a new port or slug
```

Over REST, `PATCH /api/v1/opencomputers/hosts/{id}/tunnels/{tunnel_id}` changes a tunnel in place:

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `state` | string | `active`, `paused`, or `revoked` |
| `auth_mode` | string | Change the access mode |
| `target_host` | string | Change the host the agent dials |
| `slug` | string | Change the address name |
| `rotate_slug` | boolean | Generate a new slug |
| `password` | string | Set a new password (re-hashed) |

`DELETE /api/v1/opencomputers/hosts/{id}/tunnels/{tunnel_id}` returns `204 No Content` and revokes the tunnel.

The response adds live counters you can use to check that traffic is flowing: `state`, `custom_domain`, `request_count`, `lifetime_bytes_ingress`, and `lifetime_bytes_egress`.

## Access modes

| Mode | Who can open it |
|---|---|
| `organization` | Members of your MIOSA organization only (CLI default) |
| `tenant_only` | The tenant that owns the host |
| `public` | Anyone with the URL (API default) |

> **Caution: Do not open a private service to troubleshoot it**
>
> A public URL cannot make an unavailable local service healthy, and it does not fix an authentication problem.
> Confirm the service answers on the host's own port before you change a tunnel's access mode.

## Expose a device port

`miosa device expose` publishes a port for any device kind, including a host:

```bash
miosa device expose <device> 3000
```

Use the typed `miosa host tunnel` command when you want the fuller surface - list, get, access mode, and slug control.

## What a tunnel does not do

- It does not change who owns the application. Your service still runs on your machine, under your process supervision.
- It does not remove the need for the service to be listening. The tunnel reaches a port; it does not start anything.
- It does not make the traffic private in transit beyond the transport MIOSA terminates. Set the access mode and the application's own authentication to match the data you serve.
